claims.text: A defect- and oxygen-inclusive machine-learned atomistic approach will predict conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical models.
The accuracy advantage will hold across both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Conventional analytical conductivity models for HfNbTaTiZr assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
As-cast or processed bulk HfNbTaTiZr has a typical intrinsic crystalline-defect structure.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials can be parameterized using ab initio or DFT data for refractory multi-principal-element alloys.
The training data will include defect-laden configurations and oxygen impurity environments.
Vacancies, dislocations, and oxygen atoms change local bonding and scattering mechanisms in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect- and oxygen-induced scattering changes the alloy's conductivity.
Explicitly capturing defect-induced scattering and oxygen-related impurity states corrects the oversimplification caused by perfect-crystal assumptions.
The defect-inclusive predictions will more closely follow experimental conductivity trends than predictions from defect-free analytical models.
Existing ideal-crystal analytical predictions show larger deviations from experimental conductivity because they neglect defects and impurities.
Established conductivity measurements are available for benchmarking in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen in the ranges 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Accuracy in the intermediate 200–300 K range and at other oxygen concentrations remains unestablished.
The amount of error reduction and transferability to other compositions or impurity levels are uncertain.
Deviation beyond an acceptable uncertainty margin in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
